must_remember: A streamline is an imaginary curve such that the tangent at any point gives the direction of the fluid velocity vector.
Two streamlines can never intersect, as it would imply two velocity vectors at a single point.
The equation of continuity $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ expresses the conservation of mass for an incompressible fluid.
Bernoulli's theorem states that $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho g h = \text{constant}$ along a streamline for an inviscid, incompressible fluid.
The Reynolds number $R_e = \frac{\rho v d}{\eta}$ determines whether fluid flow remains streamline or becomes turbulent ($R_e < 2000$ typically indicates streamline flow in pipes).
Torricelli's law gives the velocity of efflux as $v = \sqrt{2gh}$ where $h$ is the depth of the orifice below the free surface.
Higher fluid velocity along a streamline corresponds to lower static pressure, derived directly from conservation of energy.
For two-dimensional irrotational flow, velocity potential and stream function can be defined to analyze streamline behavior.
Euler's equation of motion forms the foundational differential basis for inviscid fluid flow before integration yields Bernoulli's theorem.
Dynamic pressure is defined as $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2$ and represents the kinetic energy per unit volume of the moving fluid.

glossary.meaning: An imaginary curve whose tangent at any point indicates the instantaneous velocity vector of the fluid particle.
The mathematical statement $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ reflecting mass conservation for steady, incompressible fluid flow.
The conservation of mechanical energy principle applied per unit volume along a streamline in an ideal fluid: $P + \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2 + \rho gh = \text{constant}$.
A dimensionless quantity used to predict flow transitions from laminar/streamline to turbulent flow regimes.
The speed of efflux of a liquid through an orifice at a depth $h$ below the free surface is equal to that of a body falling freely through height $h$.
A device used for measuring the rate of flow of a fluid through a pipe using differential pressure.
The kinetic energy density of a flowing fluid, given by $q = \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2$.
A theoretical fluid with zero viscosity ($\eta = 0$), experiencing no internal friction during flow.
A scalar function whose spatial derivatives give the fluid velocity components in irrotational flow.
A scalar function in two-dimensional flow whose constant values define streamlines.
